title: How Frogs Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore frogs and toads: recent extinctions and declines (including the Atlanta RABS fringe-limbed tree frog), what makes frogs distinct from toads, unusual anatomy (no necks, tympanum ears, tongue anchored at front, eyes pushing food down, nictitating membranes), feeding and tongue-catching physics, molting, dissection in school, the vocal sac and mating calls including release calls and amplexus, unusual reproduction (egg incubation in mouth, dad peeing on eggs, tadpoles carried on mom's back), tadpole metamorphosis and diet, defenses and toxins like poison dart frogs, threats from pollution, frog legs hunting, climate change, chytrid fungus, and the African clawed toad, cane toads in Australia, toad licking hallucinogens, and the historical frog pregnancy test. Ends with a listener mail about the Church of Satan and Anton LaVey.

segments.title: Opening banter and frog extinctions
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, credit Tracy V. Wilson's article, and discuss the Atlanta RABS fringe-limbed tree frog extinction and the rapid global decline of frog and amphibian species.

segments.title: Frog diversity and frogs versus toads
segments.summary: Size range of frog species, activity patterns, colors, which frogs do not croak, and the taxonomy distinguishing toads from frogs, including eye shape and tails in two tailed species.

segments.title: Molting, skin, and frog dissection
segments.summary: Frogs molt by eating their skin, toads versus frogs skin texture, and why frogs are used for dissection in school because their internal organs and skeletons resemble humans.

segments.title: Frog body features: limbs, necks, pelvis, eyes
segments.summary: Comparison of frog limbs to human limbs, digits, webbed feet, burrowing adaptations and estivation, lack of necks and ribs, pelvis that helps jumping, and wide-angle vision without binocular vision.

segments.title: Tongue, feeding, and eyes that push food down
segments.summary: Frog tongues are anchored at the front, enabling fast insect capture in about 0.07 seconds via non-Newtonian saliva. Frogs swallow food whole and use their eyeballs to push it down. Nictitating membranes are described.

segments.title: Ears, tympanum, and vocal sacs
segments.summary: Frogs have tympanums behind the eyes instead of external ears, which can help identify sex. Vocal sacs inflate to produce croaks and trills, and some calls resemble a screaming child.

segments.title: Mating calls, amplexus, and release calls
segments.summary: Frog mating calls, male mounting behavior called amplexus, and release calls made when a male is mistakenly mounted by another male because the sexes often look alike.

segments.title: Frog reproduction and tadpole development
segments.summary: Frogs hatch from eggs either as tadpoles or fully formed. Examples include a species that incubates eggs in the female's stomach, a dad that keeps eggs wet, and a mom carrying tadpoles on her back. Tadpoles start on plant diets and transition to carnivory during metamorphosis, and frogs eat a wide range of prey including other frogs.

segments.title: Frog defenses, toxins, and poison dart frogs
segments.summary: Frog defenses include bright warning colors and eye-spot patterns like the fire-bellied frog. Poison dart frogs obtain toxins from ants, and captive frogs are less toxic without that diet.

segments.title: Threats to frogs: pollution, frog legs, climate, chytrid
segments.summary: Frogs are fragile because their skin absorbs water and oxygen, making them sensitive to pollution and runoff. Frog leg hunting, global warming and temperature swings, and the chytrid fungus which feeds on keratin and is spread by African clawed toads are discussed.

segments.title: Cane toads, toad licking, and sign-off
segments.summary: Cane toads in Australia, the illegal toad-licking hallucinogen 5-MeO-DMT and bufotenine, the pregnancy test using African clawed toads, a listener mail about the Church of Satan, and closing remarks about contacting the show.
